rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's command banishes Iblīs in response to his threat and promises Hell for those who follow him.
rows.anchor: In response to Iblīs’s threat, God banishes him with the command Go!

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The recompense threatens Iblīs together with those he leads astray; the Quran also says jinn and humans are punished together in Hell.
rows.anchor: Hell shall be thy recompense is thus a threat addressed to both Iblīs and those whom he will lead astray

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The incitement is not a command to Iblīs; it indicates God will not interfere in the struggle between Iblīs and humanity.
rows.anchor: should not be understood as a command to Iblīs, but rather as an indication that God will not interfere

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Alternatively, the challenge exposes Iblīs’s ultimate weakness, since he has no power over God's servants.
rows.anchor: It may also be a challenge meant to reveal Iblīs’s ultimate weakness

rows.speaker: some Muʿtazilite thinkers
rows.claim: God grants Satan respite to intensify human moral challenges and thereby increase people's opportunity for reward in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: According to some Muʿtazilite thinkers, God did this in order to intensify the moral challenges facing human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan's voice can represent the various means by which he tries to mislead people, especially whispering inducements.
rows.anchor: the mention of Satan’s voice as the instrument of his provocations is more likely an allusion to Satan “whispering”

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some interpret Satan's voice as singing or music, and the verse was cited by those who prohibited singing and music.
rows.anchor: Some commentators suggest that with thy voice may refer to Satan’s misleading human beings through singing or music

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not explicitly mention music or singing, so the author favors interpreting Satan's voice as whispering rather than a direct reference to music.
rows.anchor: The verse does not, however, explicitly mention music or singing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Music's acceptability varies across Islamic perspectives and cultures; musical piety has existed throughout Islamic culture, including the song welcoming the Prophet to Madinah.
rows.anchor: music and indeed musical expressions of Islamic piety have always had a place in Islamic culture

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ajlib may mean calling forces against people or bringing all one's forces and might against them.
rows.anchor: Bear down upon them translates ajlib, which may also mean to “call forth against them”

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Satan's cavalry and infantry can mean all who commit acts of disobedience, whether jinn or human beings, since either can lead others astray.
rows.anchor: Satan’s cavalry and . . . infantry was interpreted by some to mean “all those who ride or walk in acts of disobedience”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth and children are worldly goods that can test people.
rows.anchor: wealth and children signify the good things of this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan partners in wealth and children when they are acquired or treated wrongfully or distract people from God and religion.
rows.anchor: Satan is their partner in wealth and children when either of these two are acquired or treated wrongfully

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In wealth, Satanic partnership includes inciting illicit acquisition, such as usury, or immoral spending.
rows.anchor: this may refer to Satanic incitement to acquire wealth through usury or other illicit means

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: In relation to children, Satan's partnership may involve fornication or adultery, mistreatment, misguidance, killing children, or pride in having them.
rows.anchor: this may refer to Satan’s incitement to fornication and adultery, through which children may be produced

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Satan's promises may incite wrongdoing by denying Resurrection, Reckoning, Heaven, or Hell, or by promising false intercession through idols.
rows.anchor: perhaps by suggesting to them that there will be no Resurrection or Reckoning and no Heaven or Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan's delusive promises contrast with God's true Promise, and the Quran calls Satan the Deluder.
rows.anchor: The description of his promises as naught but delusion offers a clear contrast with the repeated Quranic assertion

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: God's servants whom Satan cannot command most likely means the righteous and sincere, whom Satan cannot successfully lead astray.
rows.anchor: God’s servants over whom Satan has no authority most likely refers to God’s righteous servants

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Alternatively, servants means all morally responsible people: Satan has no authority over them, and they alone bear responsibility for their moral and spiritual errors.
rows.anchor: Some commentators suggest, however, that servants may refer to all morally responsible individuals

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's sufficiency as Guardian is affirmed elsewhere in the Quran.
rows.anchor: That God suffices as a Guardian is also mentioned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ships carrying people over water are repeatedly presented as signs of God's power and benevolence, gifts for which people should be grateful.
rows.anchor: The existence of ships that can carry human beings over the water is repeatedly mentioned as a sign of God’s Power and Benevolence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Several verses depict people calling upon God when peril befalls them at sea.
rows.anchor: This is one of several verses in which people are moved to call upon God when faced with peril at sea

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: In danger at sea, people forget their false deities, which suddenly seem useless and contemptible.
rows.anchor: the false deities whom people used to call upon are forgotten (lit. “lost”), seeming suddenly useless and contemptible in their eyes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After God brings people safely ashore, they abandon their momentary monotheistic devotion and resume earlier practices.
rows.anchor: they turn away from their momentary devotion to God alone and revert to their previous practices

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humanity, or at least most people, is repeatedly described as ungrateful by nature.
rows.anchor: That humanity, or at least most human beings, are ungrateful by nature is also mentioned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kafūr and kāfir share a root and their meanings are related in Islamic thought: disbelief is ingratitude toward God's blessings.
rows.anchor: The two meanings are profoundly related in Islamic thought, in that to be a disbeliever is to exist in a state of ingratitude

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After denouncing ingratitude, the rhetorical questions stress that the ungrateful remain liable to divine punishment and challenge disbelievers' false security.
rows.anchor: this set of rhetorical questions emphasizes their constant liability to Divine Punishment for having been ungrateful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threatened punishments recall the Quran's accounts of peoples seized for sin by stones, a cry, the earth, or drowning.
rows.anchor: The rhetorical questions in this verse invoke some of the punishments brought down on other disbelieving people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥāṣib, translated as a torrent of stones, can also mean a destructive violent wind on land.
rows.anchor: Torrent of stones translates ḥāṣib, which may also mean a violent wind that is destructive on land

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Returning to the sea means being returned to peril there after having been rescued in the previous verse.
rows.anchor: Cause you to return to it another time means that they may be returned to a situation of peril at sea

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Qaṣīf is described by some as a destructive wind at sea.
rows.anchor: Tempestuous wind translates qaṣīf, which some describe as a destructive wind at sea

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: God's honor to humanity can mean granting people authority over other creatures and making the rest of creation serve them.
rows.anchor: According to some, God has honored the Children of Adam by granting them authority over other creatures

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Distinctive human blessings include using arms and hands, intellect, discernment, speech, and the ability to know God.
rows.anchor: Others mention various blessings given uniquely to human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran connects human honor to God's creation of Adam with His Hands, breathing His Spirit into him, and giving him extraordinary knowledge.
rows.anchor: Human beings are carried over land by riding animals

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Land transport by riding animals and sea transport by ships are divine blessings for which people should be grateful.
rows.anchor: Human beings are carried over land by riding animals, which are mentioned elsewhere as a Divine blessing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The good things God provides refer to the various foods and drinks on earth.
rows.anchor: The good things provided to them refer to the various kinds of food and drink provided for them on earth

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some take God's favoring humanity above many creatures to mean above all creation, including angels, as suggested by the angels' bow to Adam.
rows.anchor: that He favored them over all that He has created

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: One interpretation distinguishes worldly blessings as God's honoring of humanity from spiritual or Hereafter blessings as His favoring them.
rows.anchor: Some commentators consider God’s “honoring” the Children of Adam as referring to the worldly blessings He gives them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imām is lexically value-neutral and can mean a guide or model; the Quran describes both righteous figures and Pharaoh with his hosts as imāms.
rows.anchor: Lexically, however, imām is a value-neutral term

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: People may be called according to the prophet, revelation, or religion they followed; wrongdoers' guides include Satan and other evil authorities.
rows.anchor: That people will be called by their leader may mean that they will be called according to the prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imam may extend to a person's spiritual leaders, religious scholars, or the religious schools of thought followed in life.
rows.anchor: By extension, the imāms by which people are called may refer to the spiritual leaders, religious scholars

rows.speaker: ʿAlī al-Riḍā
rows.claim: The eighth Twelver Imam says people are called by the imam of their time, their Lord's Book, and their prophet's sunnah.
rows.anchor: According to the eighth Shiite Imam, ʿAlī al-Riḍā,

rows.speaker: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib
rows.claim: A similar statement about being called by the imam of one's time is attributed to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.
rows.anchor: see also Q for a similar statement attributed to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib

rows.speaker: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq
rows.claim: The sixth Imam says people are called by the Imam of their time, and the Shiite Imams are called by the Prophet Muhammad.
rows.anchor: According to the sixth Imam, Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq, everyone will be called according to the Imam of their time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Twelver Shiites believe their twelfth Imam remains in occultation yet continues to guide the community and is the Imam of their time.
rows.anchor: Twelver Shiites believe that this Imam continues to guide the Shiite community to the present day

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Another supported interpretation takes imam as the book of deeds, also called imam in the Quran; the following mention of each person's book supports this reading.
rows.anchor: Their leader in this verse may also be a reference to the book of their deeds

rows.speaker: al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī explains that the book is called an imam because it is consulted as the authoritative register of people's deeds.
rows.anchor: Al-Qurṭubīsuggests that this book is referred to as an imām because it is consulted as an authoritative register of their deeds

rows.speaker: those who mention this interpretation
rows.claim: A less favored reading treats imam as an unusual plural of umm, 'mothers,' so people would be called by their mothers' names to honor Jesus or the Prophet's grandsons, or to avoid shaming children of adultery.
rows.anchor: Those who mention this interpretation indicate that this might be done for the sake of

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: An inward interpretation takes imam as the inner reality or trait defining a person, whether virtues such as generosity or vices such as hatred and anger.
rows.anchor: Still others give imām an inward, spiritual interpretation, suggesting that it refers to the inner reality or particular character trait

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The book is the full account of deeds; receiving it in the right hand signals divine contentment and in the left signals wrath.
rows.anchor: To be “given one’s book” is to be presented on the Day of Judgment with the full account of one’s deeds

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Those given their book in the right hand read it willingly and joyfully, while al-Zamakhsharī says the fearful, ashamed, regretful left-handed recipients cannot read theirs.
rows.anchor: Those given their book in the right hand read it willingly and with joy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People will not be wronged even slightly in the Hereafter, because God does not act unjustly toward them.
rows.anchor: Human beings will not be wronged in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Blindness most likely means blindness in this world: one spiritually blind to God will be blind to the path to Paradise in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Whosoever was blind in this [life] most likely means whoever is blind in “this world”

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many say such people will be even blinder in the Hereafter because repentance is possible in this world but closed there; this best fits the verse's further-astray clause.
rows.anchor: This latter interpretation fits better the context of the verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, blindness to the visible earthly blessings mentioned in the previous verse entails even greater blindness to the unseen Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Alternately, the verse can be interpreted to mean that

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quranic blindness is spiritual, not physical: it is hearts within breasts that go blind.
rows.anchor: The blindness mentioned here and in many other places in the Quran refers to spiritual rather than physical blindness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran also describes blindness in the Hereafter and says the truth-obscuring cover will be removed so sight becomes piercing.
rows.anchor: Regarding blindness in the Hereafter, see also

rows.speaker: some reports
rows.claim: One occasion report says Thaqīf sought a year's respite to continue worshipping al-Lāt before Islam, and/or asked for their land to be made sacred like Makkah.
rows.anchor: According to one report, these verses were revealed when the people of the town of Thaqīf asked the Prophet

rows.speaker: some reports
rows.claim: Another report says pagan Makkans asked the Prophet to approach and touch their idols, sometimes in return for permission to touch the Kaʿbah's Black Stone.
rows.anchor: Another report connects these verses with the pagan Makkans’ request that the Prophet come close to and touch their idols

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These reports portray the Prophet as nearly accepting the terms, but God made him firm, protecting him from moral and spiritual error and evildoers' schemes.
rows.anchor: But God then thwarted their attempt by making the Prophet firm in the face of their offer

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Double punishment in death may mean punishment in the grave before Resurrection and punishment in the Fire after Judgment.
rows.anchor: According to some, the double punishment in death refers to the punishment in the grave before the Day of Resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Doubled punishment is also described for those who lead others astray and for people whose status makes serious wrongdoing especially egregious, such as the Prophet's wives.
rows.anchor: Doubled or multiplied punishment is also mentioned for those who lead others astray

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islamic doctrine holds that the Prophet was divinely protected from sin; al-Zamakhsharī allows hypothetically that his station would make any sin especially abominable.
rows.anchor: Although Islamic doctrine holds unequivocally that the Prophet was Divinely protected from sin

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: After verse 75 was revealed, the Prophet prayed that God not entrust him to his own soul even for an instant.
rows.anchor: the Prophet said, “O God! Do not

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Those who sought to drive the Prophet out are most likely the Quraysh, whose persecution and enmity eventually drove him and his followers from Makkah.
rows.anchor: Those who were about to incite thee from the land most likely refers to the Quraysh

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Because the Quraysh did not forcibly expel him and he left by divine command, they avoided immediate total punishment; had they expelled him, divine wrath would have annihilated them.
rows.anchor: If they had expelled him, they would not have tarried thereafter save a little, meaning they would have been annihilated by Divine Wrath

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's established practice is to destroy peoples who reject His messengers, as happened to earlier prophetic communities; His response to human obedience or disobedience does not change.
rows.anchor: This is because it is the Divine wont to punish through complete destruction those who reject their messengers sent by God

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Inciting the Prophet from the land can mean trying to kill him; after the assassination plot before the Hijrah, Badr weakened Quraysh within two years.
rows.anchor: To incite thee can also be interpreted to mean

rows.speaker: a minority interpretation
rows.claim: A minority says the verse concerns Madinan Jews who urged the Prophet to leave for Syria, where their earlier prophets came from; some reports say he nearly agreed.
rows.anchor: According to a minority interpretation, v. 76 refers to some Jews of Madinah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators generally find the Jewish interpretation unlikely because this sūrah is Makkan and predates the Prophet's time in Madinah.
rows.anchor: Commentators have generally considered the connection of this verse with the Jews of Madinah unlikely

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: The verse is commonly read as covering the five canonical prayers; most take the sun's decline as the beginning of decline and the time of ẓuhr, while some take it as maghrib.
rows.anchor: This verse is commonly interpreted as alluding to all five canonical prayers

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: The period from sun's decline to nightfall can cover ẓuhr, ʿaṣr, maghrib, and ʿishāʾ; Shiites often combine the two afternoon and two evening prayers.
rows.anchor: the command to perform the prayer from the declining of the sun till the darkening of the night can be understood as a reference to completing all four prayers

rows.speaker: some Sunni schools of law
rows.claim: Some Sunni schools take the darkening of night simply as the sun's disappearance, while Jaʿfarī law waits until its rays disappear or the evening's middle begins.
rows.anchor: In some Sunni schools of law, the darkening of the night may refer simply to the disappearance of the sun

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Specific prayer-time interpretations may project the five prayers' regularity from middle Madinah back onto this Makkan revelation.
rows.anchor: the various interpretations of this verse as relating to specific prayer times may, however, be a result of commentators reading the ritual regularity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dawn recitation is the fajr prayer between dawn and sunrise, or, in one view, specifically its Quran recitation.
rows.anchor: The recitation at dawn refers to the fifth canonical prayer, namely, the fajr prayer

rows.speaker: several aḥādīth
rows.claim: The dawn recitation is witnessed by angels of both day and night.
rows.anchor: The recitation at dawn is ever witnessed by the angels of both the day and the night

rows.speaker: some Sufi commentaries
rows.claim: The prayer times also point to continuous inward prayer, the heart's remembrance and invocation of God, which is the Sufi goal.
rows.anchor: some Sufi commentaries suggest that the command to perform the prayer at these various times throughout the day is also a reference to the importance of continuous, inward prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night vigil is specifically enjoined on the Prophet, though other Muslims also perform it; most commentators consider it obligatory for him.
rows.anchor: This injunction to perform the night vigil prayer

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Calling the vigil supererogatory is figurative because it was obligatory for the Prophet, or because it is voluntary for other Muslims.
rows.anchor: The night vigil is thus referred to as a supererogatory act only figuratively

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The vigil brings merit to the Prophet and expiation to other believers.
rows.anchor: The night vigil is said to be a source of merit for the Prophet and a means of expiation for other believers

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: The praiseworthy station is understood as the Prophet's intercession, or as his place near the Throne bearing the Banner of Praise on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: many commentators consider a reference to the Prophet’s power of intercession in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The vigil has the form of canonical prayer and is usually performed in the latter night after sleep, though some allow it before sleeping too.
rows.anchor: The night vigil, which has the same form as the obligatory canonical prayers in its recitations and movements

rows.speaker: al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: Supererogatory acts expand, gladden, and ennoble the soul; night vigil is especially beneficial because one is alone with God.
rows.anchor: According to al-Qurṭubī, the purpose of all supererogatory acts is the spiritual expansion, joy, and ennobling of the soul

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer is read in the context of the Hijrah: entering sincerely means entering Madinah, and leaving sincerely means departing Makkah.
rows.anchor: As with v. 76, this verse is read in the context of the Prophet’s emigration from Makkah to Madinah

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: God directed the Prophet to migrate before Makkans could expel him, sparing them destruction for expelling a messenger.
rows.anchor: God commanded the Prophet to migrate to Madinah before they could carry out their intention

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Entering and going forth may instead refer to entering the grave and emerging from it at Resurrection, or to all situations, including the prophetic mission.
rows.anchor: The entering may also refer to the entrance into the grave at death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The requested supporting authority is for establishing Islam and overcoming its opponents; Madinah supplied political and social authority to build a Quran-guided society and spread Islam through Arabia.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is instructed to pray for authority to help him in establishing the religion of Islam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Truth and falsehood are wholly incommensurable: truth is inherently victorious, while falsehood is ultimately nothingness and vanishes before it.
rows.anchor: truth is always and inherently victorious over falsehood, which is ultimately nothingness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet reportedly repeated the verse while smashing the Kaʿbah's idols after Makkah surrendered in 8/630.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is reported to have repeated this verse continuously as he smashed the idols around the Kaʿbah

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: In context, the truth that came may mean the Quran or Islam, before which idolatry and false religion vanished.
rows.anchor: In context, the Truth that has come may refer to the Quran or to the religion of Islam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Metaphysically, Truth is God as Necessary Being or Reality, while contingent realities are falsehood, ever subject to annihilation and vanishing.
rows.anchor: Truth refers to the one certain, unchanging, Necessary Being or Reality, which is God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran and other scriptures are described as mercy in several verses; the Quran is explicitly called a cure here and implied as a cure in another verse.
rows.anchor: In several verses, the Quran and other scriptures are described as a mercy or as containing mercy

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: A hadith says God will not cure one who does not seek a cure from the Quran.
rows.anchor: Some mention a ḥadīth, “Whosoever does not seek a cure from the Quran, God will not cure him”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For those receptive to guidance, the Quran cures heart ailments such as ignorance, doubt, hypocrisy, rancor, hatred, and enmity.
rows.anchor: the Quran is said to be a cure for various ailments of the heart, including ignorance, doubt, hypocrisy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran is mercy because it helps people acquire virtue and perfected character, adorning them with wisdom and knowledge.
rows.anchor: it is a mercy insofar as it helps one acquire virtue and perfection of character

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revelation can lead wrongdoers further astray, as the Quran says elsewhere.
rows.anchor: That Divine Revelation may have the effect of leading those who are wrongdoers or iniquitous even further astray is mentioned elsewhere

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human life varies as a spiritual and moral test: God tests people with evil and good, but people often fail it.
rows.anchor: The Quran presents the vagaries of human existence as a spiritual and moral test, since God tries people with evil and with good

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People often meet blessings with disdain, arrogance, and self-satisfaction instead of gratitude, though every blessing comes from God.
rows.anchor: human beings often fail the test, responding to “blessing” with disdain

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People despair and become anxious in hardship, sometimes invoking God and then forgetting Him when hardship passes.
rows.anchor: When evil befalls human beings, they are given to despair

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The right response to affliction is patient endurance and affirming that people belong to God and return to Him.
rows.anchor: Their response, however, should be to bear their affliction with patience

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Disposition may mean inward nature or inclination, spiritual path, religion and doctrine, what one believes right and just, or one's intentions.
rows.anchor: Disposition here may be a reference to one’s inward nature or inclination

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's knowledge of who is better guided is universal, but here likely warns the Makkan disbelievers, as in another warning to them.
rows.anchor: in its specific historical context, it was likely intended as a warning to the disbelievers in Makkah

rows.speaker: many Muslim thinkers
rows.claim: The Spirit may be the source of human life, knowledge, perception, spiritual ability, and religious, moral, and spiritual responsibility.
rows.anchor: The Spirit here and elsewhere in the Quran may refer to the Spirit that is the source of human life

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Alternatively, the Spirit may be Gabriel, the angel of revelation called the Holy Spirit.
rows.anchor: The Spirit may also refer, according to some, to the Archangel Gabriel

rows.speaker: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib
rows.claim: A tradition attributed to ʿAlī describes the Spirit as an angel with seventy thousand heads, each with seventy thousand tongues praising God.
rows.anchor: According to a tradition from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, the Spirit is an angel with seventy thousand heads

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Another opinion interprets the Spirit as the Quran; the verse is also used to identify the Spirit with the realm of Divine Command.
rows.anchor: Another opinion interprets Spirit here as a reference to the Quran

rows.speaker: some reports
rows.claim: Reports say the verse was revealed after either Madinan Jews or Makkan idolaters asked the Prophet about the Spirit.
rows.anchor: Various reports indicate that the present verse was revealed in response to a group of either Madinan Jews or Makkan idolaters

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Although the verses use singular address, verse 86 is read as addressing everyone or the Prophet and community, while the final sentence of verse 87 is addressed to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: most commentators read v. 86 as addressed to people in general

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The Prophet's great bounty is his excellence among humans and his status as the seal of the prophets.
rows.anchor: in it Bounty refers to his station of excellence among human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the previous verse says people received little knowledge, this warns that even that little knowledge could be taken away.
rows.anchor: In v. 85, human beings are said to have been given only a little knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taking away revelation can mean removing the Quran from human memory and written copies.
rows.anchor: That God might take away what He had revealed is said to refer to His ability to remove the Quran completely from human access

rows.speaker: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says religion will first lose trust and last lose prayer; the Quran will then be lifted overnight from written copies and hearts.
rows.anchor: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd (d. ca. 29/650) said, “The first thing that will be lost from your religion is trust

rows.speaker: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar says the Hour will not arrive until the Quran is returned to where it descended; when returned, it will complain that people recited but did not follow it.
rows.anchor: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar (d. 74/693), the son of the second Caliph, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, is reported to have said

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without revelation, no guardian could return the Quran; the exception of mercy may mean God chooses not to remove it or restores it after removal.
rows.anchor: The exception save a mercy means either that God might choose not to remove it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These warning and exception express God's mercy in revealing and preserving the Quran in people's hearts and writing; mercy and bounty are paired elsewhere.
rows.anchor: Both the warning and the exception indicate that God’s Mercy is manifested not only in revealing the Quran

rows.speaker: some reports
rows.claim: The verse reportedly answered Madinan Jews who asked for a new revelation to prove prophethood; the Prophet said they knew the Quran came from God because its teachings matched the Torah.
rows.anchor: This verse was reportedly revealed in response to a request by some Madinan Jews

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humanity and jinn's inability to produce the Quran supports its divine origin and parallels Quranic challenges to produce revelation like it.
rows.anchor: The impossibility of mankind and jinn producing something like the Quran serves as an argument for the Divine provenance of the Quran

rows.speaker: all Muslims
rows.claim: The Quran's inimitability is a fundamental Muslim doctrine, encompassing eloquence, composition, knowledge, content, expression, and freedom from inconsistency.
rows.anchor: The Quran cannot be imitated, it is understood, in any of its aspects

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Every kind of parable means the Quran provides all indications, proofs, expression, reminders, and guidance people need for religious and worldly life.
rows.anchor: is understood to mean that He has employed in the Quran all of the indications,

rows.speaker: author
